questions.title: How can QLoRA match 16-bit finetuning performance when 4-bit quantization degrades inference performance?
questions.question_body: In the QLoRA paper, the authors acknowledge that "4-bit quantization for inference is possible, but leads to performance degradation relative to 16-bit" and that previous quantization methods "only work for inference and break down during training." Yet they claim QLoRA with 4-bit NormalFloat matches both 16-bit full finetuning and 16-bit LoRA performance. How does adding LoRA adapters on top of a degraded 4-bit quantized model recover the performance lost during quantization? Is the adapter somehow learning to compensate for quantization errors, or is there a different mechanism at play? I'm having trouble understanding why finetuning would recover information that was apparently lost during quantization.

questions.title: Understanding the Double Quantization memory savings calculation
questions.question_body: In the Double Quantization section, the paper states that for a blocksize of 64, the memory footprint per parameter is reduced from $32/64 = 0.5$ bits to $8/64 + 32/(64 \times 256) = 0.127$ bits. I understand the first term ($8/64$) comes from the 8-bit quantized constants $c_2^{\text{FP8}}$ for blocks of size 64. But I'm confused about the second term $32/(64 \times 256)$. The paper says a blocksize of 256 is used for the second quantization, but why is the 32-bit second-level constant $c_1^{\text{FP32}}$ divided by $64 \times 256$ instead of just 256? How do the two levels of blocksize interact in this calculation?

questions.title: How do gradients flow through frozen 4-bit weights to update LoRA adapters?
questions.question_body: The paper states that QLoRA "backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained language model into Low Rank Adapters" and that computing $\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{L}_i}$ requires computing $\frac{\partial \mathbf{X}}{\partial \mathbf{W}}$ via dequantization from $\mathbf{W}^{\text{NF4}}$ to $\mathbf{W}^{\text{BF16}}$. But if the base weights $\mathbf{W}$ are frozen and stored in 4-bit, what exactly happens during the backward pass? Does the model dequantize the weights to BFloat16 on-the-fly during backpropagation to compute the gradients for the LoRA parameters? Does this mean the dequantized weights need to be stored in memory during the backward pass, or are they recomputed as needed? I'm struggling to understand the exact computational flow.

questions.title: What makes 4-bit NormalFloat "information theoretically optimal" for normally distributed weights?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that the NF4 data type is "information theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights" and ensures that "each quantization bin has an equal number of values assigned from the input tensor." I understand that quantile quantization maps quantiles of the input distribution to evenly spaced quantization levels, but why does having equal numbers of values per bin make the quantization "information theoretically optimal"? Is this related to minimizing quantization error, minimizing entropy of the quantized representation, or some other information-theoretic criterion? The paper doesn't explicitly state which optimality criterion is being used.

questions.title: Why does the NF4 data type need special asymmetric handling for zero?
questions.question_body: The paper explains that "a problem for a symmetric k-bit quantization is that this approach does not have an exact representation of zero" and describes creating an asymmetric data type by estimating $2^{k-1}$ quantiles for the negative range and $2^{k-1}+1$ for the positive range, then unifying these sets and removing one duplicate zero. Why is having an exact representation of zero so critical for quantizing neural network weights specifically? Also, I'm confused about the construction: if we have $2^{k-1}$ negative quantiles and $2^{k-1}+1$ positive quantiles, that gives $2^k + 1$ values total (with two zeros). After removing one zero, we have $2^k$ values. But how does this asymmetry ensure zero is exactly representable while symmetric quantization doesn't?

questions.title: Why does adding LoRA adapters to all linear layers matter more than increasing the rank r?
questions.question_body: The paper finds that "the most critical LoRA hyperparameter is how many LoRA adapters are used in total and that LoRA on all linear transformer block layers are required to match full finetuning performance" while "the projection dimension $r$, does not affect performance." This seems counterintuitive to me. If the rank $r$ doesn't matter, why would having more adapters (each with the same small rank) help? It seems like covering more layers with small adapters is different from having fewer but higher-capacity adapters. What is it about having adapters on every linear layer that enables matching full finetuning performance? Is there a theoretical explanation for why adapter placement matters more than adapter capacity?

questions.title: What exactly causes memory spikes during gradient checkpointing with long sequences?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces Paged Optimizers to handle "memory spikes that occur when processing a mini-batch with a long sequence length" during gradient checkpointing. I understand that gradient checkpointing reduces memory by not storing all intermediate activations and recomputing them during the backward pass. But what specifically causes memory spikes in this setting? Is it that certain layers produce very large intermediate tensors when sequences are long? And how does NVIDIA unified memory's paging mechanism help — does it simply move optimizer states to CPU RAM when GPU memory is full and page them back when needed for the optimizer update step? Does this paging introduce significant latency?

questions.title: Why does the NF4 quantile formula average two adjacent quantile values?
questions.question_body:
The paper defines the NF4 quantization values as:
$$q_i = \frac{1}{2}\left( Q_X\left(\frac{i}{2^k+1}\right) + Q_X\left(\frac{i+1}{2^k+1}\right)\right)$$
where $Q_X(\cdot)$ is the quantile function of $N(0,1)$. I understand that $Q_X(p)$ gives the value such that $P(X \leq x) = p$ for a standard normal. But why is each quantization level defined as the average of two adjacent quantile evaluations? What is the intuition behind this averaging — is it trying to place each quantization level at the center of the bin rather than at the edge? And why use $2^k+1$ quantile points to define $2^k$ levels?

questions.title: Why is there orthogonality between MMLU and Vicuna chatbot benchmark performance?
questions.question_body: The paper finds that "strong Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark performance does not imply strong Vicuna chatbot benchmark performance and vice versa" and that "dataset suitability matters more than size for a given task." If MMLU covers 57 tasks including mathematics, history, computer science, and law, wouldn't a model that excels at these knowledge tasks also be better at chatbot conversations that may reference this knowledge? What fundamental difference in capabilities do these two benchmarks measure? Is the orthogonality due to the finetuning data being specialized (e.g., FLAN v2 for MMLU vs. OASST1 for chat), or is it something deeper about what each benchmark actually tests?

questions.title: If QLoRA matches 16-bit performance with 4-bit weights, where is the precision-performance tradeoff?
questions.question_body: The paper states: "Since we did not observe performance degradation compared to full-finetuning in our experiments with 4-bit finetuning, this raises the question of where the performance-precision trade-off exactly lies for QLoRA tuning, which we leave to future work to explore." This is quite striking to me. If 4-bit quantization doesn't degrade finetuning performance, does this mean that the information lost during quantization is somehow irrelevant for finetuning? Or is it that the LoRA adapters can compensate for any useful information lost? The paper also mentions that 3-bit quantization might work too. At what point does quantization actually start to hurt performance, and why? Is there something special about the finetuning process that makes it robust to quantization errors that inference is not?

questions.title: How does the empirical CDF-based quantile estimation avoid approximation errors for NF4?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that quantile quantization normally requires expensive quantile estimation, and that fast approximation algorithms like SRAM quantiles have "large quantization errors for outliers." But then it says these errors can be avoided "when input tensors come from a distribution fixed up to a quantization constant" because "input tensors have the same quantiles making exact quantile estimation computationally feasible." I'm confused: if we're assuming weights follow $N(0, \sigma)$, aren't we using the theoretical quantile function of $N(0,1)$ rather than estimating quantiles from the data? If so, why does the paper mention the empirical CDF at all? And how does normalizing by the absolute maximum ensure the weight distribution fits exactly into $[-1, 1]$?

questions.title: Why does the paper recommend Elo ratings over absolute scoring for chatbot evaluation?
questions.question_body: The paper uses both absolute scoring (GPT-4 assigns scores out of 10) and Elo ratings from pairwise comparisons, but ultimately recommends Elo ratings because the absolute scoring method has "very wide confidence intervals" due to "the lack of clear specification of scale." I understand Elo ratings come from pairwise tournament-style comparisons, but how exactly does this avoid the problem of subjective scale? Also, the paper mentions using $K=32$ and repeating the procedure 10,000 times with different random seeds. Why is $K=32$ chosen, and why does the ordering of matches matter if we're repeating 10,000 times? Is there a risk that the Elo ratings are sensitive to which pairs of models are compared first?
